title: A Computational Method to Simulate Electrostatic Actuation in Polycatenated Architected Materials
authors: Mateus Maciel Vivaldi, Alexandre F. Fonseca
abstract: A novel class of polycatenated architected materials (PAMs) has recently emerged, exhibiting distinctive mechanical properties such as stress-strain hysteresis and a geometry-driven transition between solid-like and fluid-like behavior. Although finite element models exist for conventional PAMs, none currently account for electrostatic effects. Here, we propose and qualitatively validate a computational framework to simulate the structure, dynamics, and mechanical response of electrostatically charged PAMs. Our approach successfully reproduces electrostatic actuation in close agreement with experiments, and reveals that electrostatic charges enable a reversible fluid-to-solid transition while also providing a means to estimate electrostatic stiffness. Notably, stiffness enhancements of up to sevenfold are achieved upon charging. This work expands the design space of PAMs and offers a predictive tool for actively controllable mechanical metamaterials.
summary: This work introduces a computational method using LAMMPS to simulate how electrostatic charges affect the mechanical behavior of Polycatenated Architected Materials (PAMs). The simulations successfully reproduce experimental observations of electrostatic actuation and show that charging significantly stiffens the material, enabling active control over mechanical properties. This provides a predictive tool for designing advanced, controllable mechanical metamaterials.
main_problem: The paper addresses the lack of computational models for simulating electrostatic actuation in Polycatenated Architected Materials (PAMs), which are complex mechanical metamaterials.
main_result: The proposed framework successfully simulates electrostatic actuation, demonstrating that charging PAMs can induce a reversible fluid-to-solid transition and enhance stiffness by up to sevenfold.
method: A LAMMPS-based computational framework is developed to model the structure, dynamics, and mechanical response of charged PAMs using Lennard-Jones and Coulomb interactions.
model_or_system: The system consists of PAMs, which are architected materials formed by interlocked rings (topologies J4 and T6). The simulation models the mechanical and electrostatic interactions between these rings.
key_observables: Stress-strain curves (under compression and shear), electrostatic actuation magnitude, and calculated electrostatic stiffness.
important_parameters: The study compares uncharged vs. charged states, analyzing mechanical responses across different strain regimes and topologies (J4 vs. T6).
main_assumptions: The method simplifies interactions using LJ potentials, limiting the capture to geometric/topological effects, and absolute stress values are noted to lack physical meaning due to method limitations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the point-based ring representation of J4 and T6, and show stress-strain curves comparing uncharged and charged states for both topologies under compression and shear.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the computational framework, validates its ability to reproduce electrostatic actuation, and then presents comparative mechanical analyses of different PAM topologies (J4 and T6) under both uncharged and charged conditions.
why_interesting: While focused on classical mechanics, the development of a robust, multi-physics simulation framework (combining mechanical and electrostatic forces) is highly relevant for modeling complex, interacting quantum or mesoscopic systems where external fields play a critical role.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Circular ring discretization and PAM structures considered in this study. (A) Schematic of a single ring, defined by inner radius R and thickness d. (B, D) Two views of the unit cells of the J4 and T6 topologies, respectively. (C, E) Corresponding supercells – J4 with 384 rings (952 points each) and T6 with 543 rings (690 points each) – assembled by periodic replication along x,y,z. Individual rings are color-coded for clarity in (C) and (E).

Figure 2. Compressive (A, C) and shear (B, D) stress-strain curves of the J4 (top) and T6 (bottom) PAM structures depicted in Figure 1. Insets show representative snapshots of each structure at zero and maximum applied strain.

Figure 2 displays the compressive and shear stress-strain responses of the J4 and T6 PAM structures shown in Figure 1. The J4 PAM is composed of 384 rings (with 952 points per ring), each with mass 𝑚 = 10 g, internal radius R = 0.62 mm, and thickness 𝑑 = 0.37 mm. The T6 PAM consists of 543 rings (with 690 points per ring) of the same mass (𝑚 = 10 g), but with larger characteristic dimensions (R = 4.13 mm, 𝑑 = 1.79 mm). A comprehensive listing of all simulation parameters is provided in Table 1.

Figure 3. Mechanical response of J4 (162 rings, 100 points per ring) and T6 (198 rings, 95 points per ring) PAM structures under uniaxial compression. (A, D) Stress-strain curves for uncharged structures. (B, E) Corresponding curves with electrostatic charges inserted (1 nC per point). (C, F) Linear elastic regime (strain < 2%) comparing charged (squares) and uncharged (circles) conditions. Blue and red lines represent linear fittings. (G, H) Representative snapshots of J4 and T6 structures, respectively, at zero and maximum compressive strain, for both charge states. All rings have a mass of 10 g.

Figure 3 presents the compressive stress-strain response of both uncharged PAM structures over a full 10% strain cycle (panels A, D). Although the J4 structure is known to exhibit lower compliance, the T6 architecture sustains a peak stress approximately five times higher, an effect attributed to gravitational collapse of the T6 and concurrent shear deformation in the J4, consistent with experimental observations (Fig. S8 in Ref. [18]).
